Background & Statutory Framework

The imposition of cess on exported goods has been a subject of debate and litigation in the realm of Indian taxation. The Central Government has the power to levy cess on goods under the Central Excise Act, 1944, and the Finance Act, 1994. Specifically, Section 3 of the Finance Act, 1994, empowers the Central Government to impose a cess on goods manufactured or produced in India for the purpose of financing infrastructure development. The concept of cess has been upheld by the Supreme Court in the case of Union of India vs. Delhi Cloth & General Mills Co. Ltd., where it was held that a cess is a tax levied for a specific purpose and is not a general tax.

The Road and Infrastructure Cess, in particular, has been introduced to finance the development and maintenance of roads and infrastructure in India. This cess is levied on the export of certain goods, including diesel. The levy of this cess is governed by the provisions of the Central Excise Act, 1944, and the rules made thereunder. The Central Board of Excise and Customs (CBEC), now known as the Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC), has been entrusted with the responsibility of administering the levy and collection of this cess.

It is relevant to note that the levy of cess on exported goods has been the subject of controversy, with some exporters challenging the constitutional validity of such levies. However, the Supreme Court has upheld the validity of such levies, subject to the condition that the proceeds of the cess are utilized for the purpose for which they are levied. In the case of Sahara India (P) Ltd. vs. Commissioner of Central Excise, the Supreme Court held that the levy of cess on exported goods is valid, provided that the proceeds of the cess are utilized for the purpose of financing infrastructure development.

The Development in Detail

Notification No. 42/2026-Central Excise, dated 3rd August 2026, has increased the Road and Infrastructure Cess on exported diesel to Rs. 1.5/litre. This notification has been issued in exercise of the powers conferred by Section 3 of the Finance Act, 1994, and is applicable with effect from 3rd August 2026. The notification specifies that the increased rate of cess shall apply to all exports of diesel made on or after the specified date.

The increase in the rate of cess on exported diesel is likely to have a significant impact on the export of diesel from India. Diesel is a major export commodity, and the increase in the rate of cess is likely to affect the competitiveness of Indian exporters in the global market. The increase in the rate of cess may also lead to an increase in the cost of production for Indian exporters, which may be passed on to the consumers.

The notification also provides that the increased rate of cess shall be levied and collected in accordance with the provisions of the Central Excise Act, 1944, and the rules made thereunder. The CBIC has been entrusted with the responsibility of administering the levy and collection of the increased rate of cess. The notification also provides that the proceeds of the cess shall be utilized for the purpose of financing infrastructure development, as specified in the Finance Act, 1994.

The increase in the rate of cess may also lead to an increase in the cost of production for Indian manufacturers who use diesel as an input. The increase in the cost of production may be passed on to the consumers, which may lead to an increase in the prices of goods and services.

It is relevant to note that the increase in the rate of cess on exported diesel is not a new levy, but rather an increase in the existing rate of cess. The existing rate of cess on exported diesel was Rs. 0.5/litre, and the increase in the rate of cess to Rs. 1.5/litre represents a three-fold increase. The increase in the rate of cess is likely to generate significant revenue for the Central Government, which shall be utilized for the purpose of financing infrastructure development.

The increase in the rate of Road and Infrastructure Cess on exported diesel to Rs. 1.5/litre is a significant development in the realm of Indian taxation. The exporters may also argue that the increase in the rate of cess is not in line with the principles of international trade, as it may lead to trade distortions and affect the balance of trade.

Background & Legal Framework

The Income Tax Act, 1961, provides for various deductions and exemptions to encourage certain activities, such as donations to political parties. Section 80GGC of the Act allows a deduction for donations made to a political party or an electoral trust. Section 270A(9) of the Act specifies the circumstances under which a penalty can be imposed, including when the taxpayer has misreported or underreported their income. The Supreme Court in the case of CIT vs. Eli Lilly and Co. (India) Pvt. Background & Statutory Framework

The Goods and Services Tax (GST) regime, introduced by the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 (CGST Act), has undergone significant developments since its inception. Background & Statutory Framework

items.title: ITAT Pune Quashes Reassessment Based on Wrong Facts and Borrowed Satisfaction
items.summary: ITAT Pune quashed reassessment for incorrect recorded facts and lack of independent application of mind, and deleted Section 68 additions. The post ITAT Pune Quashes Reassessment Based on Wrong Facts and Borrowed Satisfaction appeared first on TaxGuru .
items.body:
Background & Legal Framework

The Income Tax Act, 1961, empowers the Assessing Officer to reopen assessments under Section 147, if they have reason to believe that any income chargeable to tax has escaped assessment. However, this power is not unfettered and is subject to certain conditions and safeguards, such as the requirement to record reasons for reopening the assessment under Section 148. The reassessment proceedings must be grounded in a genuine belief that income has escaped assessment, and not merely on suspicion or conjecture. The concept of "reason to believe" has been elucidated by the Supreme Court in various judgments, including the landmark case of Raymond Woollen Mills Ltd. vs. ITO, where it was held that the Assessing Officer must have tangible material to support the formation of a reasonable belief that income has escaped assessment.

Furthermore, the principle of "borrowed satisfaction" has been deprecated by the courts, which means that the Assessing Officer cannot merely rely on the satisfaction of another authority, such as the Audit Party, without applying their own mind to the facts and circumstances of the case. The Assessing Officer must independently apply their mind and form a reasonable belief that income has escaped assessment. This principle has been reinforced by the CBDT through various circulars, including Circular No. 549, which emphasizes the need for the Assessing Officer to record clear and cogent reasons for reopening an assessment.

In the context of Section 68, which deals with the treatment of unexplained cash credits, the Assessing Officer must demonstrate that the cash credits are not explainable by the taxpayer, and that the same are therefore, taxable as income. The onus is on the Assessing Officer to prove that the cash credits are not genuine, and that the same are liable to tax under Section 68. The taxpayer, on the other hand, must provide a satisfactory explanation for the cash credits, failing which, the same may be treated as income liable to tax.

Facts of the Case

The present case before the ITAT Pune involved a reassessment proceeding initiated by the Assessing Officer under Section 147, on the ground that certain cash credits were not explainable by the taxpayer. The Assessing Officer had recorded reasons for reopening the assessment, which were purportedly based on a report of the Audit Party. However, upon examination, it was found that the reasons recorded by the Assessing Officer were based on incorrect facts, and that the same did not demonstrate a genuine belief that income had escaped assessment.

The taxpayer had provided explanations for the cash credits, which were not satisfactorily considered by the Assessing Officer. The explanations provided by the taxpayer were based on documentary evidence, which was not rebutted by the Assessing Officer.
